metadata.note: The Delaware and Hudson's Ausable Branch, 21 miles southwest from Plattsburgh up the Ausable valley to Au Sable Forks. It was built in 1869 by the Whitehall and Plattsburgh Railroad as what was meant to be that company's main line toward Albany; the through route went along the Lake Champlain shore instead and this was left a branch, never extended beyond the Forks. It carried the Peru Iron Company's ore, the output of the J&J Rogers works at Au Sable Forks, farm goods from Peru bound for Montreal and New York, and tourists into the Adirondacks, with two passenger trains a day each way. Its ending is unusually well documented: the D&H withdrew the passenger trains in 1929, and the painter Rockwell Kent, who lived at Au Sable Forks, came home from Greenland to find them gone. With the lawyer Philip Wager Lowry he took the railroad to the New York Public Service Commission, which ordered service restored in November 1930 - then reversed itself in 1931 as the D&H's income collapsed, and the trains stopped for good. Freight lasted into the late 1970s and the rails came up starting in 1981; those years are not drawn here, per the passenger-only rule. Station order: South Junction - Laphams Mills - Peru - Harkness - Rogers - Ausable Forks.

metadata.not_yet_sourced: The exact month in 1931 when the restored service was withdrawn again (TIME reported the Commission's reversal on Sept 7 1931). Also unsourced: the opening month in 1869; the headways before and after the 1873 D&H consolidation, which are assumed to match the documented twice-daily service; whether the Montreal and Plattsburgh lease of 1870 changed who actually crewed the passenger trains; and the alignment by which the line reached Plattsburgh before the Champlain shore main line opened in 1875.

segments.note: Restored service. After the 1929 withdrawal the painter Rockwell Kent, who lived at Au Sable Forks, returned from Greenland to find no train, and with the lawyer Philip Wager Lowry took the D&H to the New York Public Service Commission on behalf of a valley of some 10,000 people; the railroad answered that one train had made 50 round trips without a passenger and averaged two fares a trip. The Commission sided with Kent and ordered service resumed in November 1930 - the service drawn here - then reversed itself in 1931 as the road's net operating income fell, ending Ausable Forks passenger service permanently; riders were directed to buses on the parallel concrete highway. Note on the drawn years: app.js treats a segment's end year as inclusive, so the 1873-1929 and 1930-1931 segments abut and the interruption is NOT visible on the slider. That is deliberate rather than an oversight - trains did run during part of 1929 before the withdrawal and during part of 1930 after the November restoration, so no single year on this map is service-free, and ending the first segment at 1928 to force a visible gap would assert an absence of service in 1929 that is not true. Freight continued into the late 1970s and the rails were lifted starting 1981, but a freight-only era is not drawn on this map.
